newsitem.title: USA: Compaq unveils new products, reports strong second quarter.
newsitem.headline: Compaq unveils new products, reports strong second quarter.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp. Thursday unveiled a new line of personal computers and cut prices in a bid to compete with Dell Computer Corp. and other rivals, and reported earnings that beat most expectations on Wall Street.

Compaq cut prices on its older Deskpro corporate desktop computers by up to 22 percent and introduced 13 new Deskpro models starting at aggressive prices of $1,199 for a machine with a multimedia Pentium MMX chip, reflecting its new strategy of lowering costs by using more direct distribution.

"Every company has its defining moments of transformation," President Eckhard Pfeiffer said at a news conference in New York. He said Compaq, the world's largest PC maker, was making other manufacturing models obsolete.

The Houston-based company's new strategy means it is building products based on customer orders, which lowers costs by cutting out some distributors and reducing inventories. Later this year its remaining distributors will also configure and build products for Compaq customers.

The build-to-order strategy is meant to compete with Dell, Gateway 2000 Inc. and other companies that are pressuring PC makers with their lower prices and lower costs. Dell is the fastest growing of the major PC makers.
Dell, Gateway and other direct marketers take orders over the telephone or the Internet from consumers and companies for machines that are built-to-order.

But Compaq is still a formidable competitor. Its second-quarter operating earnings of $422 million, or $1.48 a share, surpassed most analysts' estimates. The results excluded a charge of $208 million related to its acquisition of Microcom Inc.

Including the charge, Compaq's net income fell to $214 million, or 75 cents a share, from $267 million, or 97 cents a share, a year earlier. Sales jumped 25 percent to $5 billion from $4 billion and unit shipments climbed 42 percent.

Compaq said the charge knocked 73 cents off its earnings per share. The writeoff was related to technology acquired when Compaq bought Microcom, a maker of modems and other gear based in Norwood, Mass., for $280 million in April.
Analysts had expected Compaq to earn $1.39 a share from operations, according to First Call, which tracks estimates.
Its stock, which ran up in the 10 sessions ahead of the earnings report, fell 87.5 cents to $120.125 on Nasdaq.
"The numbers roughly came in line; gross margins were a little higher," said David Wu at ABN AMRO Chicago Corp. "There is nothing really outstanding to note."

Compaq executives said the price cuts and aggressive pricing on new models would not hurt earnings. In the second quarter, gross profit margins jumped to 25.3 percent of revenues, up from 24.5 percent in the first quarter.

"You are not going to see our margins going down because of our pricing on new products," Chief Financial Officer Earl Mason said. "It's not a price war, it's about passing on efficiencies to our customers."

But Compaq's moves sparked a reaction from other PC makers. Hewlett-Packard Co., anticipating Compaq's announcement, said Wednesday it plans to cut prices on many corporate PCs up to 24 percent. International Business Machines Corp., the biggest PC maker after Compaq, said it plans to remain competitive but did not give details.
The changes by Compaq could ripple further through the industry the way its big price cuts did five years ago, changing the competitive landscape, analysts said.
But Compaq executives and analysts said many PC makers would not be able to win a price war with Compaq without hurting profits since their costs will not be as low.

"If people start cutting prices below the levels we are at, they will start cutting into operating margins," said Lou Mazzucchelli, a Gerard Klauer & Mattison analyst. "Compaq can lower prices without hurting margins," he said, noting it has been working on its new manufacturing methods for almost two years.

Compaq's new PCs includes seven Deskpro 2000 models with Intel Corp. Pentium MMX multimedia chips, ranging from 166-megahertz (MHz) to 233MHz and hard drives as big as 3.2 gigabytes, priced from $1,199 to $1,899.

Prices for its Deskpro 4000 models range from $1,389 to $2,089. The six new Deskpro 4000 models, geared more toward network environments, are available with similar processers and memory, Compaq said. Compaq said its prices range from 6 percent to 8 percent lower than similar models from Dell.
Compaq cut prices on the older Deskpro 6000 by 9 percent to $2,419. The machines have a 200MHz Pentium Pro processor, 2.1-gigabyte hard drive and 32 megabytes of memory.
It also cut prices on lower-end machines. For example, a Deskpro 2000 PC with an Intel 166MHz Pentium chip will now go for $999, a cut of 16 percent, the company said.
